scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Though now a symbol of Aragonese pride, the Jota’s roots are contested, with some accounts placing its origin in 12th-century Valencia as a funeral dance before it migrated north to become a high-energy celebration.
This is Jota Aragonesa. 18th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (xfDMK5Ibs_s)
Title card: Jota Aragonesa · Spain · 18th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Jota is believed to have 18th-century roots in Aragon, though legends suggest a 12th-century origin in Valencia.
The term derives from the Mozarabic 'šáwta' (jump), linked to the Latin 'saltāre'.
It gained significant prominence following the Spanish War of Independence.
on_screen: Map: Spain · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Jota serves as a generator of local identity and social cohesion.
It is performed at festivals, weddings, and religious celebrations, and has been adapted for zarzuelas and theatrical stage productions.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform in pairs or groups, utilizing small, leaping steps and rapid footwork.
Arms are typically held high, and castanets are used to mark the rhythm.
The style varies from the airy, leaping Aragonese version to the more sober, sharp movements of the Castilian style.
Watch for Leaping steps.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (xfDMK5Ibs_s)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Couples or groups, circular paths
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is driven by stringed instruments including guitars, bandurrias, and lutes.
Regional variations include the use of bagpipes (gaitas) in Galicia and Asturias, and dulzainas and drums in Castile.
Listen for the Guitar, Bandurria, Lute, Dulzaina.
The pulse is 3/4 or 6/8.
A lively, percussive sound dominated by the bright, metallic strumming of bandurrias and guitars, punctuated by the sharp click of castanets.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers typically wear traditional regional costumes.
In formal or theatrical settings, these are elaborate and specific to the dancer's home province.
In informal social settings, dancers may wear everyday clothing.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Pedro Nadal ('el Royo del Rabal'), Mariano Malandía, and José Oto, who is considered the most important singer of the Aragonese Jota.
Variants exist across Spain, including the Jota Castellana, Jota Navarra, Jota Montañesa (Cantabria), and the Philippine Jota, which incorporates bamboo castanets and rondalla music.
The Jota is related to the Fandango and shares roots with the Renaissance 'Branle' and various 'sauts' found in the Pyrenees.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Jota Aragonesa is sibling of Fandango: Shares rhythmic and structural characteristics.
Jota Aragonesa is influence of Bolero: 18th-century boleros influenced the development of the Jota.
